opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hannah. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won't be linked to your name.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sounds good. I think about this stuff a lot anyway, so it's nice to say it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great productivity tool. My cash-flow models that took two days now take an afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it really stalls here, I've moved into data-centre work a bit early. That's fine. It's a growing market either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep building out the data-centre side. Do a short course on power grids, because power is the thing that decides where these sites go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly amused that I might be over-preparing.

S0.say: It's a great productivity tool. Models that took two days take an afternoon.
S0.think: If AI stalls here, she pivoted a bit early, but data centres are growing either way.
S0.do: Keeps building her data-centre work and takes a short course on power grids.
S0.feel: Calm, slightly amused she might be over-preparing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the analysts who learn the tools will be fine, and the ones who don't will slowly get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's roughly what I'm already seeing, just slower. The junior analyst seats are going. I worry a bit for the people I'd have mentored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan, less rush. I'd mentor the one junior we still hire and make sure they learn the tools from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little sad for the next lot coming through.

S1.say: Analysts who learn the tools will be fine. The ones who don't will slowly get squeezed.
S1.think: It's what she already sees, only slower. Junior seats are going and she worries for them.
S1.do: Sticks to her plan at a slower pace and mentors the one junior still hired.
S1.feel: Fine, a little sad for the next lot coming through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the routine part of property analysis is gone and we should be honest about that. I'd also say we need proper retraining, not just speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old job, the spreadsheet part, is basically done. The part that's left is judgement: which town has the power, the water, the planning approval. That's where I've put myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask to lead our data-centre deals officially, with a title. Build relationships with power companies and local councils, because those are hard for an AI to fake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit tense, but I saw it coming. That helps.

S2.say: The routine part of property analysis is gone. We need real retraining, not speeches.
S2.think: The spreadsheet part of her old job is done. What's left is judgement on power, water and planning, which is where she has moved.
S2.do: Asks to lead data-centre deals with a proper title and builds ties with power companies and councils.
S2.feel: A bit tense, but she saw it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say there's huge demand for AI infrastructure and real estate has a big part to play.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if AI matches skilled professionals, it matches me too. My bet is clients still want a person to blame when a site goes wrong. I'm good at this, so I'd probably be one of the last. But probably isn't certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be one of the last. What makes you sure of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure. I'm good, and I'm early. But that's what everyone good thinks, isn't it? I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bank as much of the bonus as I can while the market's hot. Talk with my husband about paying off a big chunk of the mortgage. Keep a list of firms that would hire me if mine cut back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert. Not scared, but awake at night a bit more.

S3.say: There's huge demand for AI infrastructure and real estate has a big part to play.
S3.think: AI matching professionals means it matches her too. She bets she'll be among the last, but knows everyone good thinks that.
S3.do: Banks bonuses, talks with her husband about paying down the mortgage and keeps a list of firms that might hire her.
S3.feel: Alert. Not scared, but awake a bit more at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a serious plan for people who work with their hands, because they've been told for years they were safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much from the last one. If anything, robots building data centres faster means more sites to pick. My worry is the same as before, plus watching everyone else get hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast version. Maybe give more to a charity that helps retrain people, because it would feel wrong not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the world. Oddly, a bit steadier for me.

S4.say: We need a serious plan for hands-on workers who were told for years they were safe.
S4.think: Robots building data centres faster means more sites for her. Her own risk is the same as in the fast version.
S4.do: Sticks to the same plan and gives more to a charity that retrains people.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the world, a bit steadier for herself.
